newsitem.title: CROATIA: UN certifies vote in Croatia's last Serb enclave.
newsitem.headline: UN certifies vote in Croatia's last Serb enclave.

text.p: The United Nations on Tuesday certified postwar elections in Croatia's last Serb enclave as free and fair, despite technical irregularities that forced voting to be stretched over two days.

Former rebel Serbs in Eastern Slavonia/Baranja voted on April 13-14 for the first time in six years in Croatian elections, winning 11 of 29 municipalities in preparation for the region's reintegration in Croatia this summer.

Unofficial results indicated Croats who voted in absentia captured a narrow majority in the region's main town Vukovar, which was demolished in an infamous Serbian siege in 1991 near the end of Croatia's war for independence from Yugoslavia.
"On the basis of the information available to me.., I formally declare the certification of the elections," said Jacques Klein, head of the U.N. transitional administration in the enclave (UNTAES).
"Final results are not expected to change the provisional results (announced last Sunday)," Klein, an American diplomat, said in a statement issued in Vukovar.
He noted "technical difficulties" which afflicted some of the voting, especially the late delivery of ballot materials by Croatia's state electoral commission.
But, Klein said: "No intimidation, violence or electoral impropriety was observed or reported before, during and after the voting and counting.

Klein said the turnout was unexpectedly high, with more than 70,000 people -- mostly Serbs -- voting inside the enclave and more than 56,000 -- mainly Croat war refugees -- casting absentee ballots elsewhere in Croatia.

Both Croatian and Serb officials have expressed general satisfaction with the voting in the enclave, which was seized in a 1991 insurrection by pro-Yugoslavia Serbs who drove out their Croat neighbours.
The elections coincided with voting for municipal and county assemblies and the upper House of Counties of the Croatian parliament staged throughout the rest of Croatia.

President Franjo Tudjman's nationalist party regained control of the upper house and almost all 21 county assemblies and most town councils but lost to or deadlocked with centre-left opposition blocs in some cities including Zagreb.

"The successful holding of...elections (in Eastern Slavonia/Baranja...is an historic milestone in the peaceful reintegration of the region...and in creating conditions for reconciliation and return (of war refugees)," Klein said.

"They open the way, after six years of war and conflict, to address the real human tragedy of war by enabling all displaced persons to return... We cannot change the past, nor can it be forgotten, but the elections are a new beginning..."

UNTAES has already restored some economic and human contact between Serbs and Croats, although ethnic enmity still runs deep, and obtained minority guarantees for Serb residents in Croatia's nationalist and highly centralised republic.

Klein said more than 90 percent of Serbs who were in the enclave when a treaty for its peaceful reintegration was signed in November 1995 remained today, contrary to forecasts of a panicky mass exodus to nearby Serbia.
"The people of the region demonstrated in a dignified, constructive way (by voting) that they wish to remain in Croatia and participate in political life," said Klein.

Still, Western monitors believe up to a quarter of the Serbs may leave for Serbia in coming months because they are unreconciled to renewed Croatian rule or fear retribution from returning Croat refugees.
Klein, keen to ease a still palpable apprehension about the future among local Serbs, will turn now to sewing up loose ends before Croatian state authority is reinstated in July.

He wants to set up a "soft-border" regime with Serbia to ease travel for normal personal and commercial reasons, get an accord on dual Yugoslav-Croatian citizenship for Serbs, and demilitarise the Danube River border strip.
